why: Minimise the maximum group range: after sorting, groups can be taken as contiguous runs, and 'can three groups of range <= D cover everything?' is checked greedily, each group starting at the smallest uncovered value and taking everything within D. Binary search the smallest D that needs at most three groups.
hints: The order of A does not matter. Sort it: what shape do the groups of an optimal answer take?

Fix D. Open a group at the smallest uncovered value v and put everything <= v + D in it; repeat. If at most 3 groups are needed, D works (split a group further if you need exactly three, since n >= 3). Larger D needs no more groups.
Binary search D in [0, max - min]; each check is three bisect_right jumps (or one O(n) scan). O(n log n).
pitfalls: Groups must be non-empty, but fewer than three greedy groups are still fine: splitting never raises a range.
Do not try every pair of cut points in O(n^2) when N is large.
constraints:
• 3 <= N <= 105
  • -109 <= A[i] <= 109
